_comment: The attestation gate the Confidential samples put on their KMS key. A sample's setup
script drops this _comment key (KMS rejects an unknown top-level key), fills in the
placeholders and calls kms:PutKeyPolicy with the result:
<ACCOUNT_ID>      the account the key lives in
<POD_ROLE_ARN>    the pod's dedicated EKS Pod Identity role, which carries no
identity policies of its own, so every permission it has on this
key is written here
<EXPECTED_PCR17>  the measurement the policy generator predicted for the approved
pod's Cedar policy
The shape is allow-on-match plus explicit-deny-otherwise. Three things make
attestation, rather than possession of the credentials, the boundary:
1. KeyAdministration lists its actions instead of using kms:*, and leaves out
kms:Decrypt and kms:ReEncryptFrom. ReEncryptFrom matters as much as Decrypt: it
would let a key administrator re-wrap the layer key under a second, ungated key
and then decrypt it there.
2. AttestedDecryptOnly is the only allow for kms:Decrypt, and it is conditional.
3. The two denies apply to every principal. A negated condition operator is also
true when the key is absent from the request, so a Decrypt that carries no
attestation document at all is caught by both of them.
Sources, all public: the kms:RecipientAttestation condition keys in the AWS KMS
Developer Guide, 'AWS KMS condition keys for AWS Nitro Enclaves'; 'Cryptographic
attestation support in AWS KMS' in the AWS Nitro Enclaves User Guide; Decrypt and its
Recipient and CiphertextForRecipient parameters in the AWS KMS API Reference; the
default key policy and its 'Enable IAM policies' statement in the AWS KMS Developer
Guide, 'Default key policy'. Which measurement index holds the policy, and the
PCR8:ServiceName form rather than a raw PCR8 value, come from the Amazon EKS User
Guide, 'Cedar policies'.
